utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the Chamber trusts that your health has improved over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I feel a lot better, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, witness. We will now continue the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, first, Your Honour, we received a copy of a document in the meanwhile. We got the statement from Mr. Hangatsori, an UNPROFOR soldier, and we downloaded it in the e-court system. And we have a number for it, and I would like to offer it as evidence. And it's number DD00-1118 in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand correctly. You're offering this as evidence. You wish to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I'm just not aware that the statement was -- has at this point been shown to the witness, or whether conclusions from it have been put to the witness. But maybe I'm -- of course, I'm happy for parts of the statement to be put to the witness, or for the statement to be shown to the witness, but I don't think it's been done yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the Chamber doesn't have a clear recollection of the statement having been put to the witness, so would you briefly put whatever it is that you wish to the witness from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The portion I'm interested in is just one sentence, on page 2 at almost at the end, "[In English] French officer showed me. I thought it was something like 81, 82-millimetre shells. I haven't seen a tail-fin." [Interpretation] I showed this to the witness, and earlier he had said that during the interview the Prosecutor had shown him another situation report, I guess, where there is mention of this mortar being shot and not a gun being shot, a cannon being shot. I forgot to note on what page this was, but I'm sure we could find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, just put to the witness, again, the two issues: What kind of weapon it was, and where did the firing come from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, last Friday, I'm sure you remember that we talked about the incident of December 22nd, 1994 at the flea market; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we talked about your own analysis?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And what were your conclusions regarding the weapon the shell was actually shot from?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance, it was a 76-millimetre shell fired from a gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that there were UNPROFOR soldiers who were on the site carrying out their own crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. After we completed our analysis of the crater, they proceeded with their work. I think that they had arrived in the meantime and started their own examination. After we compared our findings, in terms of direction from which the projectile had come, it was established that these two findings coincided. I think that they were identical with respect to the direction of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding the weapon, the weapon that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one moment, Ms. Isailovic, just let him say what direction was that. Witness, what direction was that from which the firing came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was fired from the area of Trebevic. I can't remember exactly the exact azimuth that we measured, but I believe that it was south-easterly direction; closer to the south, but generally south-easterly direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, last Friday you said that upon arrival the Prosecutor showed you the analysis made by UNPROFOR where the weapon mentioned was a mortar and not a gun or cannon. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an analysis as far as I was able to understand from this document. It was an UNPROFOR report on incidents, and it mentioned that at that time and on that location two projectiles exploded, most probably 82-millimetre mortar shell. Therefore, it was not an analysis. It was just a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you were shown a statement last Friday, a statement made by an UNPROFOR officer, Mr. Hangatsori, who was there on site. I will read to you what he said in that statement, and it has to do with the findings regarding the weapon. "[In English] According to the shrapnel a French officer showed, I thought it was something like 81, 82-millimetre shells. I haven't seen a tail-fin."

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is my following -- the question is the following: Do you remember the statement by this person that was shown to you last Friday? It was in English.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I said that our analysis showed that this analysis, or rather, the report does not correspond to the factual state of affairs. Based on fragments, we established that it was a 76-millimetre projectile. UNPROFOR did not collect these fragments, and I don't know what their analysis was based upon. Following the on-site investigation, these fragments were collected; and after the on-site investigation, the team took this -- these pieces as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that things would have happened according to what Mr. Hangatsori said in his statement?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even in theory. There is no theoretical possibility that it was a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to offer this statement as evidence, DD00-1118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just say that you know the witness who made the statement has not been called and, therefore, there's been no opportunity for cross-examination on these conclusions and, therefore, it would clearly go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not different in any way from the usual hearsay statement, but let me hear you further. You were developing another argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I was merely saying that the fact that the witness has not been called and not cross-examined would go to the weight of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, therefore, we can admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's been done in the past in this Court, so I'm just merely stating that the weight should be afforded appropriately to this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Because I make a distinction between this document and the ones that we have been marking for identification, in the sense that those we are marking for identification is that the witness doesn't know anything about the document. That is not the case here. The difference is in the opinion as to the -- the type of weapon and where it came from. The Chamber will admit it and, of course, we take account of the submissions that you made about the weight to be attached, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel? Counsel? Ms. Isailovic, since you are the person to cross-examine, I will put my question through you and I would like to you ask the question, put the question to the witness if he can clarify a bit more why he does not think that there is not even a theoretical possibility that the grenade was a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, I'm sure you heard this question, but I will reformulate it. Why -- could you give us your reason that why you totally would exclude the fact that this grenade or this projectile might come from a mortar?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons lie in the evidence collected on the spot, including the trace left on the surface by the projectile as well as on the basis of the collected fragment pieces. These fragments were analysed in detail. This can be subjected to extra analysis, if necessary. They were analysed by the CSB in Sarajevo, and the analysis relied on both the traces and the fragments and it was established beyond doubt that it was a 76-millimetre shell. There was not a single evidence found on the spot pointing to the origin of the projectile being a mortar shelf of any calibre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because of this shift in the examination, I'm going switch topics, too, and change my questions. And so we'll continue with the incident of December 22nd, even though I had other questions in mind. Let's talk about December 22nd. Do you remember an affidavit that the Prosecutor asked to you sign last Friday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, please allow the court deputy to assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That statement will be Exhibit D101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, before you move on, you say that the analysis relied on both the traces and the fragments and it was established beyond doubt that it was a 76-millimetre shell. That's more an assertion. What is there about the traces and the fragments that established beyond any doubt that it was a 76-millimetre shell, because are we have not technical people. So you have made this assertion, but I, speaking for myself, would need to be told what was there specifically about the traces and the fragments that led to the conclusion that it was a 76-millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, there was probably some markings on the pieces of fragments. Each projectile bears a marking, so there was probably a fragment of the marking on the physical evidence. At this point, I cannot remember exactly what was written on it; but based on the markings and based on the characteristics of very specific fragments, we arrived at the conclusion some of the fragments were totally irrelevant, but there was some characteristic ones. And some that bore the markings served as a basis for establishing the type and the calibre of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you a part of the team that carried out this examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll continue along the same line. In -- in the report everything that goes toward this conclusion [Realtime transcript read in error "exclusion"] written down, right? Sorry. It's not "exclusion" that the interpreter wrote, it was "conclusion." So I'll reformulate. The whole logic regarding how you analysed the origin of the shot is actually written down in the statement?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Its had been decisively stated in the report which kind of projectile was involved on the basis of the fragments detected and retrieved from the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... finding, but the whole logic, the rationale, the procedure that you used to actually to arrive to this finding or conclusion. I would like to know whether the whole thought process is also included in the report, the whole logic?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typically, our report contained a description of individual fragments, and this is followed by an opinion. In this particular case, the opinion was as I just explained to you a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll come to this in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the Court's information, the report and related reports of this incident have been admitted into evidence with the spreadsheet. It was part of the documents that the witness reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have been developing a view that there is a problem with the way we admit documents under the e-court system. Well, just in this particular instance, because you say that was part of the spreadsheet. But it wasn't shown specifically to us this report, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I didn't use it in my chief because the procedure we adopted was to save time as we had done in previous instances: for example, with the W-28 and also with Dr. Mandilovic. And the witness reviewed these reports in my office and, therefore, we produced -- I produced the affidavit that he signed. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you seen this report, Ms. Isailovic? Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have seen it and we're going there, and I'm going ask that, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're going to ask questions about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, please, we are going to linger on this incident of December 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would ask my case manager to call up the document that was tendered and accepted as P314.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this is part of this official report dealing with the incident that occurred on December 22nd, 1994. So, first, we have a map, a map where you actually annotated the direction where the shot came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, in my view, when we admit documents globally without the party adducing evidence on the parts thereof, I think the party should state what the document consists of. Of course, it's on the e-court and we can track it down, but I think it would be more than helpful if we developed a practice for a party to identify the various items in a document that is admitted as a whole, so that we can determine whether any one of those items warrants further questioning. But I imagine you're going to tell me this is all on the -- is it on the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was indeed going to say that I have attempted to identify exactly what the witness has seen. If, Mr. President, you're suggesting that when this procedure is employed we could read out in court what is on the spreadsheet, then I would agree that would be a useful idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that at least should be done, if it's not overly long at any rate. So do we have the document that you wish?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're waiting for it to be displayed. We actually pressed on -- gave the order for the -- for this document to be pulled up on screen, but we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Court Deputy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I understand it's taking a while because it's a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, while we're waiting for the map to be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember those documents you saw with the Prosecutor and which are on that list that you actually signed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. President. But if there's a problem with the e-court, I do have hard copies that can be shown to the witness to assist the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be helpful, yes. Please provide the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I just inquire through the Court whether the Defence wants to show the witness the report that he himself compiled? Because I understand my learned friend was talking about a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, the map first; and then the report, P315. Maybe the way we could proceed in the following fashion: The Prosecutor could please give us the hard copy for the map, and we will pull up the report on screen. It might take a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It sounds like --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, here comes the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have the map now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you -- this is the map that you actually annotated yourself. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please come and help you to work the electronic pen, so that we could show something else on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, this green arrow represents the direction that the shell was actually shot from, according to your findings. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It was the direction with a degree of or a margin of possible error, because it was impossible for to us determine it 100 per cent correctly; therefore, we could have an error of plus or minus 5 per cent. But this is the direction from which the shell came, based on the measurements made at the place of impact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it fair to say that you were not able to determine the distance?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were not trying to establish the distance in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So could you please circle Colina Kapa on this map.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please enhance the map, zoom in? It should be somewhere around here. I don't know exactly, but Colina Kapa, in my view, is around here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Don't you see any letters on this map or inscriptions on the map?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place where I put my marking says "Bogusevac." As for Colina Kapa, I can't see it. I am unable to find such an inscription. I don't know what the number 3 is supposed to mark.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom a bit for, if possible.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. Colina Kapa, on the map, is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please circle it? Just draw a circle around Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And do you see Vidikovac on this map?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vidikovac is the place to which the cable car could eventually take you from the old town before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Letter A on Colina Kapa; letter B on Vidikovac.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, Your Honour, I would like to offer this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D102.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'm going to ask my case manager to call up document P315 on screen. This it the report written by your boss, I guess, at least it was signed by your boss, and we talked about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, you see the report on screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please move to page 2 of the B/C/S version. The English version is only one page long.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, is this the entire report regarding the crater analysis, the direction of the shot, and the nature of the -- of the projectile that fell on the flea market? Is everything included in your report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at page 1 a part of the text is illegible in this report we drafted, because at page 2 we only see the opinion as to the type of projectile. I think there is a part of the text missing where we have the description of some characteristic fragments based on which we made the conclusion that could be seen on page 2. We never drafted reports in this way, that we would provide an opinion without any basis. We always described the characteristics and it's traces which led to us a certain conclusion. There were some reports of ours in which we described the fragments, but we also state in some of them that it was not possible to establish the type of projectile based on the traces found.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could we go -- could we please zoom in on the first page in the B/C/S, or look at the first page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, this is also very difficult for me to read the document, and sometimes it's very hard to know exactly what is written in these documents, in the documents that are offered here as evidence. But the missing part here, according to you, would be the crater analysis. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The part that is missing is the analysis of traces and evidence collected. In the bottom part, we cannot see the part of the text which was supposed to describe the characteristic traces found on the fragments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness: Are you able to read the B/C/S? It's not very legible. If you are, would this provide the missing information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think so. Because in the part that I can read, I can only see that it is stated there that we have been forwarded material for expert analysis. You can see the date when that took place and the address, or rather, the name of the street. I can read out for you the things that I see, not the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, never mind. Yes, Ms. Isailovic. Just a minute, Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, witness, there is something that I don't understand. Are you challenging the authenticity of this document, or are you saying that there are portions that can you not read and that because of that you cannot exactly know what is included in the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not question or dispute the authenticity of this document, but this is a very poor copy and there is part of the text which is simply invisible. I don't know why. But the originals of these reports I believe can be found with my former department of KDZ. This is an authentic report, but the copy you have is very poor and you simply cannot see an entire portion of the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is this -- when you made an affidavit about a document, it was about the document, this document, the way it is written here and the way it was presented here?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was shown this document, and we established that a part of the text is invisible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the boss -- your boss, you know, who signed the document, do you think that he could have contributed something to help us know exactly what the document was all about? Because you didn't seen the document in the first place. It's your boss that signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question appears to be ambiguous. You have asked him whether he thinks that his boss could have contributed something to help us know exactly what the document was all about. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a document that we have, like the document it we have here on the screen, cannot help Chambers discover anything; discover at least the analysis that was made after the incident. And it was a very important incident because it is in the schedule, in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not my question. It's probably a translation or a language problem. Do you mean to ask whether his boss might be able to say something that could clarify the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Because the witness here did not sign the document. It's another person who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what is your answer to this question, Witness? Do you think your boss might be able to add something that would clarify the document, the missing parts of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the quality such as the one you have here, no one could help you in assisting you to read. It is correct that my boss had things to do with this report, but can you also see my initials on the second page, which means that I worked on it as well. Based on a copy as poor as this, no one could explain anything further to you. The only way to go to would be to come up with a better copy of the report so as to be able to see the missing part; and, perhaps, if I may add, I could tell you that my boss did not attend the on-site investigation. He probably saw the traces on the fragments during the analysis at our department. I don't know exactly whether he was there at that moment; but as our boss, he was supposed to supervise our work. Therefore, it is likely that he saw the traces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, according to you, the analysis would be in this missing part of the page, in the invisible text?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to save time, so we agree on the missing part. Thank you. Now, we will continue with the same incident and the same affidavit?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to call on screen the document P317.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, last Friday, you said that the casualties and the eye-witnesses were not your main concern when you visited the site of the incident.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representatives of my department, that is the technical staff, did not deal with such things. It wasn't our task on site. There were other team members who were tasked with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yet you certified the content of statements that were collected on site by your colleagues. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certified the authenticity without going through each and every word; because once drafted, I did not see the documents subsequently. I can confirm the authenticity of the documents, but I did not go through it chapter and verse.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we please have page 2 of this document on screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, could you please take a close look at this document and tell us who actually collected the statements, the name of the colleague that actually collected the statements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you who took statements. There's a signature here of the person who took the statements, but I don't know who it was. There's only the name of a witness, of the person giving the statement; but as to who took the statement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as a police officer, do you find it normal not to have the name of the officer who actually wrote down the statement made by a witness? Do you find it normal that the name of the person would not be written out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mean written above the signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, or elsewhere, but somewhere at least. Because in our national jurisdictions, we have different systems and different procedures regarding, you know, how reports are made by an officer, a police officer. And I'm asking the witness to tell us where in this document we can see that the -- an official officer actually wrote down this official report.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about that. I see the statement had been taken in the CSB on the 11th of January, 1995 by Salih Luksija who then signed his statement. I can't tell you anything about the things that you're asking me about now. I cannot furnish an answer that would satisfy you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm happy with all answers; it's not the problem. The question here is to check the authenticity of this document and you certified it. You certified it with -- by oath, right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But it concerns the authenticity. As for the contents, it will be best to ask the person who provided the statement and signed, because that person stated what is contained.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'll ask my case manager to call up page 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, does the same thing apply to this document, or could you tell us in this case who actually wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless there is a name that I can read on the document, I cannot tell you who took the statement for any of such documents. I can only confirm what I can see written here. As for the authenticity, this was the template, the form that we used. And at bottom, you were trying to say that at the bottom there should be a name printed out legibly, but I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you already confirmed the authenticity of these documents, but I'm asking you what basis you use to actually authenticate these documents?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the form of the document itself and the signature of the witness. Whether it is the witness's authenticate signature, well, I can't say because I don't know the witness, but the document as we see it here corresponds to the form we used. The witness's signature should be authentic, I believe. As for whether he was telling the truth or not, I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you're saying that this document is -- has a correct format. Is that it? You're saying that the format of the document is perfectly normal, according to you. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have lost the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I also repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's the witness's answer that should be repeated, not the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the format of a statement. In the preamble, some basic information is given us as to when and where the statement was taken; then the statement itself as made by the witness is noted down. It's then read back to the witness, and the witness signs it is as its own. So not even the person taking the statement can verify and stand by, but only the person giving the statement can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's move to page 10, for example, now. So, it's -- it's a bit blurry, but we can still need the name of the officer who actually wrote down the statement collected from a witness, and we can even see the name of the registrar, or clerk. So here's my question: The format of this statement, do you think that it is more legal or more -- is this format more legal than what we saw earlier?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to me to determine what is legal or not. I'm not a legal person. You can see the name of the witness here, the person who took the statement, Sulejman Pilav, and the recording clerk; however, the contents of this statement can only be verified by the witness who stated where was at the time if the incident and where he went. No one can now check that any longer, so this should be taken as the statement of the witness saying and describing the incident. As far as the legality is concerned, I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So let's go back to the list, document P327, the list that the Prosecutor asked you to sign. Witness, we have the schedule here on screen. Do you remember this schedule that you signed Friday?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at number 1. You remember that Prosecutor showed you this criminal investigation file?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So here's my question, and if need be, we will actually call up the entire file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Look, Ms. Isailovic, I don't think we need to call up the entire file; but I wanted to ask you, what is it that you would be asking the Chamber to conclude in relation to these many documents to which you have been referring? What is your submission on it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is my submission. Here we've been presented with a great number of documents that are on a schedule. Personally, of course, I studied them very carefully, and I noted that for a number of documents the witness that we have here did not actually take part in the investigation, and I'm trying to determine, to help you determine the weight you should actually give to this evidence. This evidence is offered through this witness, even though -- well, it's up to you, of course, to find out. But I'm trying here to demonstrate -- I try to help you in assessing what weight should be given to this witness's deposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would your submission be that we should attach little weight to it for the reason that the signature of the -- the investigating officer is not sufficiently clear, or the name of the investigating officer is not identified?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, these are elements and parameters that have to be there for documents to be legal and depend -- for each document, my submission is different. But regarding this witness, he actually authenticated this document. All these documents are offered through him, and I wanted to check about him exactly what he knows about all of these documents regarding all these documents, because he is actually testifying in terms of the authenticity of these documents. And if I can go on, for document 1 and 15, for example, I am offering to the witness that he did not even take part in all these investigations regarding 1 and 15. So I'm asking him whether he is just testifying on the apparent form, on the form that the documents have but not on the substance of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, how would you respond to that submission, that for the reasons that she has outlined the Chamber should not attach much weight to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course, arguments regarding weight depend upon the entirety of the evidence, as the trial proceeds. What the witness has done and what he has confirmed under oath and what has never been -- which has always been maintained by the Prosecution is that the witness has confirmed the validity or the authenticity of these records. It doesn't require the witness to have participated in an investigation to render a record valid. We did the same exercise with Dr. Mandilovic, who may not have performed surgery on you particular patients but testified that these document were valid medical records. Of course, my learned friend is entitled to put her argument as to the weight of the documents, but in terms of the procedure for admission, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I don't think we're not dealing with that. It's just weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. And, in any case, the fact that the witness did not participate in an investigation again goes to other arguments of weight. We will have witnesses that have participated in these investigations; and once the evidence has come in, then only then the proper arguments can be put regarding weight. But in my submission, these documents are valid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will be bringing other witness who will be able to speak more directly to the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: We have already brought other witnesses, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic. Do you still plan to go through all of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, Your Honour. It's just documents 1 and 15, because there I would like to ask the witness whether he actually took part in the investigation. We have the documents anyway, and we can display them or you could look at them if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Here's my question, Witness, please. You see the document on the first page under number 1. On the next page, there is also a document that is mentioned under number 15. Did you take part in these investigations; and if so, in what manner?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we waiting for a document to be shown?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Normally, the document is displayed.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said on Friday, as well, what our capacity was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interrupting you right away, because I'm asking you a very practical question. On this list here, there are two numbers: Number 1 and the number 15. It's the first document and the last document on this schedule, and here's my question: Did you participate in the investigation; and if so, in what manner? You signed this list on March 2nd. You signed that in front of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the technical part of the investigation involving the collecting of evidence and subsequent analysis, I did take part. This involved the collection of fragments, as I said, on the scene; however, I did not take part in taking statements. I did not take photographs. I did not go to hospital to take a statements of people. That was not part of my job. However, when it comes to collecting physical evidence and the analysis of the direction of the projectile and compiling a report, I -- I did take part in that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see that time is flying, but I you really believe that we have to continue with this cross-examination. I need some extra time because I believe that this witness is very important. He's saying something that needs to be demonstrated in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much time are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm -- I might be ready to -- not to go into other questions, but I think I need at least half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll give you 20 minutes. Well, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm unable to be here for the rest of the day because I'm preparing a witness for tomorrow. All I wanted to say is that I trust that Your Honours received the report from the OTP regarding Mr. Hansen, as Your Honours had requested for today, and I just wanted to make sure that there was no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I have questions to ask about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So if you could come immediately after the break, and we can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the Chamber thanks for the report that you have submitted on Captain Hansen and the unknown UNMO. The report indicates that have you been in contact with Captain Hansen. He has been difficult to reach by phone, but you have reached him. He has given some information about the -- the UNMO, who witnessed this particular incident, and a request has been made by the Prosecution for assistance from the Kenyan government to locate the UNMO, because it was believed by Captain Hansen that he came from that country. Now, as for Captain Hansen himself, you see that he has stated that he would not be available to testify from the 6th to the 15th of March or during the last two weeks of April; and for that reason, you have asked whether he would be able to testify on the 2nd of April, and you're awaiting a response. I'm not particularly happy about that aspect of it, because what we're running here is a court, an international court of law. We are not operating a social activity. It's not as though he is being invited to a dinner party, and I did not find acceptable the wording that he would not be available to testify from a particular time to a particular time, without any explanation being given for that unavailability. So I'd like to hear you further on that, because the Chamber is of the firm view that Captain Hansen should come to testify one way or the other; and the sooner, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm unable to tell Your Honours what the reasons are for him stating that he is unavailable during those times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you not speak with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I did not myself speak with him, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Our investigator. At the time we got that information, it was before Your Honours had requested that he come testify, and it was at that time -- we had already started speaking with him when the information when the issue arose, and so it was before Your Honours had made that request. So we got the information -- he stated that he was unavailable during those times, but we did not pursue it any further; that is, I don't know whether it was for professional reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should have been pursued subsequent to the Chamber indicating its interest in having him testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The reason we didn't pursue it further, Your Honour, is looking at the schedule ahead of us, looking at the additional information that we would like to have available to us and to the Trial Chamber when he comes to testify, so that his -- that he doesn't have to come more than once, and finally looking at the issue which is really involved -- the issue which is at issue here, which is, in our view, narrow and specific, we thought that having him come by April 2nd would accommodate all of those things; that is, that it -- it would be in sufficient time to address the issue. We would then have in hand all of the necessary information so that his appearance would be the most fruitful possible. So it was not our judgement that it would be necessary to bring him here sooner than that. So that is why we didn't pursue it further and press him to come sooner. Our schedule is also, as I've indicated, we have a lot of dates that are now quite committed to witnesses who cannot come other times for various reasons, who have been rescheduled in the past. We have a very, very tight board, and even this date we have to bump somebody off this date so that he would be able to come testify. So are all the reasons why we left it as it was and selected that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course, it is open to the Chamber to -- to call him at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, under the rules, it's open to the Trial Chamber only if the Trial Chamber makes a finding that is in the interests of justice. Because ordinarily since are in the Prosecution case, it the Prosecution who has the prerogative to call the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It must be clear to you that we consider it an important matter and in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I certainly do. I would not imagine, Your Honours, that would it with be the interests of justice to call him next week as opposed to the week following. I don't see the possible justification for rushing. As I have indicated in our memorandum, we are awaiting clearance for documents which will be relative to his testimony. I think it would be fruitful if we were able to identify this unidentified UNMO before he came. All those things, I think, would be beneficial. And I certainly don't -- I do not appreciate, myself, and I could be enlightened on this, but I don't see why it would be necessary to bring him here next week, for example. I think if we bring him here April 2nd, it seems to me that would be -- from what I can tell, that would be sufficient to address the concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in any way making his coming contingent on the identification of the UNMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. No. I would add one other thing, Your Honours, and that is -- we can talk about this at another time. But, of course, we would like to be able to cross-examine the witness when he comes. I'm happy to do -- allow him to tell his story or do a kind of direct examination without any leading, but we would then, of course -- from the point of view of the Prosecution, we would like to have an opportunity, since we are not really calling this witness, but it's the Trial Chamber is asking that he be called, that we be allowed to cross-examine the witness. And if we're not, that may factor into whether we actually do call the witness, and perhaps we would leave it to the Trial Chamber to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the Chamber calls the witness, he is open to examination by all the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's what I would think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But at this stage, what I had done was to invite you to call him. Now, if you don't want to accept that invitation, then you should say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will accept the invitation as long as we have the ability to cross-examine him, which is critical. In light of the information obtained, we cannot -- we do not think it would be fair and in the interests of justice at all, if they were not allowed to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is for the UNMO or for Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is for Captain Hansen. Our position on the UNMO is undetermined right now, because we don't know who it is and we haven't spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel. If you call him, he would be your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, just because he's our witness, just because we call him, and he is our witness, does not mean that we cannot cross-examine him. There are situations where we would be allowed to cross-examine our own witness, and I think is one of them. But where we have been invited, I see this invitation as we are accommodating the interests of the Trial Chamber and facilitating bringing this witness here as quickly as possible during the Prosecution case, but normally we would not call this witness. It was not our intention to call him in this case. We would not call him, so it seems to me unfair if we're -- if we call him and then we are not allowed to cross-examine him. And if that ends being the position, I would have to say we will probably not call him, and we would leave it to the Trial Chamber to call him. We're just trying to accommodate Your Honours to get him here and to have him testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is well appreciated, but my understanding is if you would call him you would examine him in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm happy to do an examination-in-chief to allow him to tell his story, but then I would -- I would ask that we be allowed to challenge that story and to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because normally the basis for that in the common law system and, indeed, in the cases that have proceeded with that procedure here at the Tribunal is that you -- there is an a contradiction between the evidence being given by the witness in court and a previous statement that. That would not be the case here. But I'm not unsympathetic to a procedure where the Prosecution utilizes the means at its disposal to secure the attendance of the witness, and the witness is then called by the Court and then is he open to examination by all the parties. But I think that would have to be made clear to the witness that he's being called by the Court, even though it's the Prosecution that is utilizing the means at its disposal to secure his attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, and I would be very happy to work with that solution, and Your Honours could decide whether you wanted to do the direct examination or you wanted leave it up to us to do it. I would note, of course, Your Honour is correct. I share Your Honour's understanding how things would work in a common law system; but, of course, in a common law system, the Court would not ask the Prosecution to call a witness. That would not happen; that is a civil law system attribute. When we mix and match here, we also have to accommodate our interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to respectfully ask for you take one thing into consideration when arriving at your ruling. This witness was on the list of the Prosecution witnesses; and at moment when the Chamber was asked to allow for certain witnesses to be removed from the list, his name was stricken out. So, initially, he had been witness proposed by the Prosecution; but due to the request posed in terms of time restrictions and concerns, this witness was removed from the list. So this should be taken into account when you reach your ruling. In my view, this person can only be a witness for the Prosecution and subject to the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But by what means can you oblige the Prosecution to call a witness that it doesn't wish to call? Or by what means can the Defence be obliged to call a witness it doesn't wish to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are of the position that the Prosecutor should renew its witness list. He initially had been made part of the witness list at first, and they should redo their list. As for me as counsel and the way I should try and tackle this, that is a delicate matter. But that witness was one of their witnesses, and at that time he was not a hostile witness. It turned out he was a hostile witness at the moment when a certain document surfaced, and I have faith in the Bench in trying to come up with the proper solution, but I merely wanted to express our position here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you believe you can secure his attendance on the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I certainly hope so. And if that turns out to be a problem, then that is when we will begin to push and insist. But I'm hoping that date will be fine, and I except to know -- I actually thought I would know by now. But I expect to know today or perhaps tomorrow, and I will inform Your Honours as soon as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: By Wednesday at the latest, and you bring him here and he will testify as to the witness called by the -- by the Bench, so that he would be available for examination by all the parties. Whether the Bench will lead him is another matter or whether we will get a statement from him on the basis of which he may be examined is something that we'll decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just so Your Honours know, there is no an OTP statement from way back of him that pertains to this issue, and, of course, we'll make all of this available to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: , Now there is another matter that I want to discuss and for that I want to go into private session, and this requires your presence, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm staying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand the technicians are asking that the next break be for 30 minutes, as they have more work to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And, Ms. Isailovic, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sure you remember that earlier we were talking about the schedule that you signed, and I would like to see the document that is under number 1 so that we could look at it together, so I'm asking my assistant to call it up. We will look at all the pages. I submit that you did not participate to this investigation at all, and you can answer this after having seen all the pages in the document. But maybe the date of the investigation can help you decide on the answer you will give.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the basis of the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We are waiting for the English version to be called up, and we can look at all the -- all pages in the B/C/S version. Could you please first take a look to see whether your name is included in the investigating team? So let's move to page 2. Let's move to page 3 now. We have the signature of the person who wrote the report, but this is not your name, right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the investigating team?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't at the location of the explosion in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move to page 4. Now page 5. Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This report that we have just seen, can you tell us if you took part in the drafting of this report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to the next page, please. Unfortunately, we have a problem with the display, so we're asking for the registrar to please help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, this is the report on the traces in the explosion. I mean, that was your field of competence, right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move to the next page, please. Next page again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, here, it -- the person who signed this document is still your boss, right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He signed it, but I think the initials at the end of the document are NB. Perhaps we can zoom in on those and then I may be able to tell you who the person was who processed and completed the report. Yes, NB. It an a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The name uttered by the witness was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nedim Bosnic did not sign the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Nedim Bosnic didn't sign the document either, neither did you, witness. So you were not involved in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably participated in the analysis of traces and in assisting my colleagues. In Kosovo, we always did teamwork.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness should be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, please speak into the microphone. Will the usher please see that the mics are adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: There are still a few pages to this document. We can continue to peruse through them, look at all pages, one after the other, and you can see whether you were involved in any way in this investigation. And we're talking about the investigation that is in the schedule under number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please move, move on. Move to the next page and the other pages, so we can just scroll through the document until the end of the document, please. Here maybe we need to ask a question to the Prosecution. We have the medical report which may be inadvertently put in document P313. I don't really know how this medical report ended up in this document, in Exhibit P315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. My learned friend is right. It should not be there. The ERNs quite clearly indicate that the last page should be 00375126; and 5126 is the map, the sketch. So as was stated on Friday, the witness did not review medical records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Anyway, Witness, what did you certify in relation to this report?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning this event, I confirmed that such an incident indeed took place, and I presume I assisted my workmates in the analysis of traces. We worked in teams. I know that this incident took place on that day and at that time. There was an explosion of a projectile at that spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, regarding the document that we find under number 15 in the schedule, it was -- which is Prosecution document P326. Here again, we have the English version on the screen. Witness, could you please take a look at the date and tell us if you actually took part in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please look at the whole file? Because there was so many incidents, it's impossible for me to remember what happened on which date.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We're getting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll through the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Here we have mention of the Simone Bolivar elementary school in Dobrinja. Did you take part in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I review the whole set in order for me to give you a definitive answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Just one question: Last Friday, did you really look at all this before actually signing the list and the schedule?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But I don't recall specific dates; therefore I cannot attach an event to a date. There were so many incidents, and we are just focussing now on one section; therefore, I cannot vouch for, say, the dates. That's why I wanted to look at the whole file.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, we have just scrolled through the entire file, and last Friday you certified what -- what did you certify? Can you please tell is what you certified, you certified last Friday, regarding this document?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So after reviewing the file, I said that all the specific cases dealt with there was authentic and that the incidents indeed took place at the times specified.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the documents contained in each case file, which confirms that whenever I was present at the scene there's my name there, and vice versa there is no mention of my name when I didn't attend the scene. But I, nevertheless, remember most of the events that took place in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, in your statement, because it's -- according to Rule 92 ter, we have your document -- your statement of February 28th, 1996, P310. And there is one sentence in this statement that we talked about Friday. We talked about the explosion that occurred on June 28th, 1995 on the TV building. Do you remember having talked about this last Friday?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I was involved in the on-site investigation following the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: There's something that I would like to show you in this respect; 65 ter document 298. It's an UNPROFOR report, and there is a sketch that I'm interested in. It's a sketch which, according to the report, would represent the shell that was seen falling on the building. This is the report that deals with this event of June 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please call up page 3 of this document. That's page 2, but we would like to have page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the sketch on the screen? Thank you. So we have a sketch, and the legend on the B/C/S version there is only the legend.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please have on the screen the translated legend in B/C/S, since the original was English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So now we have the two documents side by side. Witness, please, last Friday you made a correction to your statement, and you said that on the scene you found no fragments of engine and no fragments of rockets. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a correction to the statement. The same thing is stated in our report following the incident, that these fragments of the engine and other pieces had not been found.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. So we agree on that. I think you made a slight rectification to your statement, not to what actually happened. What we have here on screen is the projectile that was seen by UNPROFOR members, and they drew a rough sketch of this projectile. According to what you found on the site, could this sketch actually correspond to whatever you found on the site?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The physical evidence retrieved on the spot originate from an air bomb. And this sketch, one might say, generally shows one of the forms of air bombs. They are manufactured in a variety of forms, so one might say that this is something approximate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Here you see the dimensions that were given by the person who actually made the sketch. It would be 60 centimetres long and 20 centimetres wide. Do you believe this is acceptable in terms of dimensions?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These dimensions are unacceptable. I was talking only about the shape, which is accept to a certain extent. As for the size, especially the width, I don't think that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What do you base yourself on to say that? What do you rely on to say that the dimensions are not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not acceptable because a 20 centimetre diameter of a projectile and the amount of charge to be packed inside could not possibly have caused such devastation at the place of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what would be say would be the more acceptable dimensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at least twice the diameter of the one stated here, so that means 40 centimetres or more. The wall of the TV building that was penetrated was made of reinforced concrete over 30 centimetres thick, and the reinforced concrete was -- bars were over 15 millimetres in diameter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you should be bringing your cross-examination to a close now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, if I could just ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On site, you did not find the parts that would have normally been part of a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter correction: It is just "air bomb," not modified.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fragments were found on the spot, probably originating from the body of the air bomb. As I said, no parts of the motors and adapters were found which otherwise were always found under such circumstances, which means that a modified air bomb has a head, engines, and an adapter, an adapter to serve the bomb and the propelling engines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: How many casualties were there after the explosion on the site? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that a fellow police officer was killed who is from the same area where I came from, and we grew up together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And in your report, his name is mentioned as being the victim. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at the report, because I don't know -- don't remember what is stated there. We received input, information along with the request from the CSB, specifically how many casualties there were and their names. We would just rewrite this information. We didn't collect this type of information at the scene. We were involved only in the technical aspect of on-site investigations, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to offer this exhibit -- tender it, but I have a problem. This 65 ter number corresponds to another document, which was marked for identification, D31, and it's this document without the drawing. It's been marked for identification as D31, but it's this document without the sketch. And I would like to tender the -- the entirety -- the entire 298 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're inclined to admit it, Ms. Isailovic. The question is the confusion that seems to exist in relation to D31. Is the court deputy able to offer any clarification?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, D31 is marked for identification. It was done so on the 1st of February and it's an UNMO Sector HQ, and that particular document was marked confidential or is marked confidential. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So how does this drawing relate to the UNMO report?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judges, this -- here we have the entire report. I don't know how we ended up with these two pages that we have already used, because after the fact I did some research. And under another 65 ter document, 298, I found the entire report supplemented with this sketch, if I may say so. And since we have discussed the sketch with the witness, after the discussion, the witness confirmed what was in this drawing. The drawing actually corresponds to what was in the report of the UNMOs. It show what the UNMOs actually saw that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You want to us admit the entire document, not just the specific pages that you just referred to in your cross-examination? I'm beginning to become a little wary - and this applies to the Prosecutor, both parties - about admitting these global documents without seeing the specific items that are included in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Defence is also in the same position. As time goes by, you know, we discover pages that actually serve or case, and I would like the entirety of the report to be tendered. This sketch is part and parcel of the report. It's the report made by Captain Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think in the interests of consistency, we'll have do it. We have been doing it for the Prosecution, then we will also do it for the Defence. So we admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It will be partially confidential because of the report which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that be Exhibit D103 under seal, partial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, since you're still in the courtroom, I'd like to go back with you on the question of this bomb which fell on the TV building. On page 48, line 8 and 9, you said that neither the head nor the engine or the motor, nor the adapter of this bomb was actually found. So if I understood exactly what was said, this would have been an air bomb but not a modified air bomb. Is that what you said, that it was just an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was a modified air bomb; however, where its engine ended, I don't know. If I may, I would just like to add one sentence. There is certain contradiction in the description given by UNPROFOR. It says that the width was rather big and the projectile was rather short, which means there is a discrepancy between the sketch and the verbal description. I believe that this projectile, like all others, when we were dealing with modified air bombs that landed on the city of Sarajevo - and more than ten of them landed on the city of Sarajevo. I don't know how many of them landed in Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija - in this particular case, it is true that we didn't find fragments of the propelling engine, which only demonstrates how unreliable this weapon was, and it shows its imperfection in terms of design. In my view, these engines properly fell off during the flight. That's the only logical explanation that I can find. Let me just add one thing. What we found at the scene were fragments originating from the body, or rather, the head of a modified air bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, just a few issues I want to deal with. Firstly, I just want to take you back to when counsel for the Defence was talking about: The report of the 24th of May, 1995, and also the report about an incident at the Simone Bolivar school on the 18th of June, 1995. Firstly, do you remember being asked questions about those two incidents?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you told the Court that you had not participated in the on-site investigations for those two incidents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I would like to review again, because I believe that I did take part in the investigation regarding the school. But I would need to look at the report. It should bear my name. Because according to the name of the school, it doesn't ring any bell. I cannot remember many schools were targeted by these kinds of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, just for the moment for this question, irrespective of whether you were there or not, what you confirmed on Friday, in other words, what you signed were documents -- you saw documents from those two incidents, and I want to ask you today: Do you confirm that those documents are authentic, valid documents from the Sarajevo CSB or the Ministry of the Interior, irrespective of the contents?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can fully confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, may I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, how can he confirm what you want him to confirm, "irrespective of the contents?"
