Aren't the content an essential part of the document, in fact, the most essential part, or are you suggesting that he confirms the authenticity just on the basis of the appearance of the document, that it has a reference to the relevant government department and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is why there are documents pertaining to incidents that the witness did not himself investigate or conduct an on-site investigation. But given his experience in the ministry, he has seen such documents, and the signing of the spreadsheet essentially serves two purposes. There are documents that he himself drafted. There are incidents that he himself went to, and there are others that he did not. But for all of those documents, he has, at least by signing the spreadsheet, confirm the their authenticity and their validity, in terms of the form, in terms of the process. And the reports for the Simone Bolivar incident have been already tendered into evidence, the police reports, the on-site investigation report, through -- through another witness. So yes, for -- for the Simone Bolivar school, he has authenticated the validity of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It comes as a bit of a surprise to me that the documents mentioned on the spreadsheet were not all of the documents that related to incidents in which the witness had participated himself. I don't know if I can suggest that for further occasions, we are being informed of whether the documents sought to be admitted relate to documents that -- relate to incidents, sorry, that the witness himself did participate in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, firstly, the statements of the witness clearly indicate which incidents he was involved in. Secondly, the process that we've employed here, the Prosecution has asked to use, is the same as that what we did with Dr. Mandilovic and another doctor; namely, that they did not necessarily perform those specific operations, they did not necessarily write the medical report, but they were able to confirm the validity of those reports, the authenticity of those reports. So my submission is based on the precedents that has been set in this Court what I undertook with the witness is simply a reflection or following that precedent, and I've -- it's clearly maintained in my submission those incidents that he himself was involved in are clearly represent-- that those incidents that those incidents that he was involved in are clearly indicated in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I appreciate what you have just said, but my difficulty, nevertheless, is that when you present a list on the spreadsheet of 15 documents which you seek to have admitted into evidence, then I must say that I was led to believe, perhaps wrongly, that all of these 15 documents were relating to incidents in which the witness himself had taken part in the investigation. Now, if you then tell us that some of these 15 documents are only sought to be admitted for the purpose of -- in relation to this witness for the purpose of confirming their authenticity, then I think I would have liked to have known that when you presented the spreadsheet with all the documents for admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, there's been no deliberate intention to mislead the Court. I submit that my questions to the witness and what is contained in the statements provides, in my submission, clearly what incidents he was involved in and what incidents he was not involved in. These documents are being admitted into evidence and, of course, what weight is attached to those documents depend upon the other evidence that is coming in and the context of the case that will proceed and also what has taken place through other witnesses. But this witness is simply, at least with respect to these two incidents, attesting that these have valid materials from the CSB, authentic materials from the CSB and, therefore, sufficiently reliable for them to be admitted into evidence. But if this procedure is adopt in the future, it can be stated clearly on the spreadsheet or it can be orally stated that -- stated where the incidents -- whether the witness has also been to the incidents. That can be undertaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would agree and I would suggest that you do it in the spreadsheet directly, because we will be returning to the spreadsheet later on in the trial; and at that moment, we may have -- I've forgotten but perhaps not be completely aware of the documents on the spreadsheet are now admitted only for the purpose of authentication and which are not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President -- Your Honour, yes. I would also add that in my questions to the witness in chief, I did, in my submission, set the foundation by asking whether he would in the course of his business come into contact with other reports from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sachdeva. Witness, that concludes your -- Oh, you have not finished. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I have -- may I have Exhibit P317 brought up on the screen, please. Can we just move to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember being showed this page in the examination by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see there on the bottom right-hand side, there's a signature?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see on top of the signature, there is a phrase in B/C/S, "izjavu uzed"?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Statement taken by." It means that the signature there is that of an official, or rather, the official who took down the statement from the witness. The statement was supposed to have been taken by a -- from the eye-witness, and the note-taker merely registered his participation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I just want you to focus on that signature for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'd like the exhibit -- well, could we go to page 12 of this exhibit, please, and the bottom right hand -- yeah, be zoomed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, do you see there a signature on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Now, before having a look at the writing, I wanted to take the floor, even though my -- I have no more time. Maybe I wasn't crystal clear. I believe with our witness we're going to have a look at the graphical expertise of the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, exactly what is your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that now my colleague -- I'm avoiding him doing this because I find it unacceptable, but it's up to you to decide. To compare myself, I had the opportunity to do this, but precisely this is up to a graphics expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear. Let us hear what he is going to ask the witness. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just -- well, can I ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see on the bottom right-hand side, do you see -- or, firstly, a signature there?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see a name on top of that signature?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nurija Nakas, or Makas; N or M.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And my question to you is: Does the signature appear to you to be the same signature that you saw a moment ago in the second page.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have both documents on the screen at the same time and then I can tell you what I see, but the authenticity would need to be confirmed by a graphology expert. He could tell you whether these are the same signatures. I can only tell you whether they look the same to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. For what it is worth, do they look the same to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have both documents on the screen, if that is not too much of a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have both documents on the screen. Do you wish to press on with this? I don't wish to rule it -- rule it out, but I'm not certain whether it is going to advance your case, if he says that the two signatures do look the same. Well, we do have the two signatures now. What is your comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, this is the same signature, but, as I said, only a graphology expert could tell you whether they indeed are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I also want to ask you a question about the 22nd of December, 1994 incident at the flea market. You remember being asked questions about that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you told the Court that the determination was that the projectile used was a 76-millimetre cannon shell; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On that day in the investigation, did you -- well, did you undertake the investigation with other police officers from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would first make a team and then that team would go out onto the location, and each member would do his part of the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the investigation, was there consensus among the members of the team about the type of shell that was -- that impacted at that time at that space?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, no statements are given of such a nature during the examination. An opinion is given only own after an expert analysis of traces and fragments had been carried out. One can guess as to the degree of probability, but no official statements are issued before a report is drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: At the scene was there -- do you remember if there is was a view or if there was a conclusion that the projectile used was that of an 82-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unofficially, what we thought at the spot was that the calibre was 76. No one mentioned the possibility of a mortar shell 82-millimetre calibre. Concerning the team police, or actually, what I'm telling concerns the team of the police who were at the location, excluding UNPROFOR; and if I may add, UNPROFOR did not share their opinions or views with us. They made their own analysis, although I don't know on what basis. They only photographed the traces and fragments on the spot, and they did not take them with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, lastly, Witness, At the beginning of cross-examination, the Defence were asking you about your experience in crater analysis, and I want to ask you: From when you joined the police, or the KDZ, up until the conclusion of the conflict, roughly, how many crater analyses did you personally undertake?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to say. Many. I analyse craters even nowadays. Whenever I see traces in the asphalt, I think about them, I analyse them unintentionally. It is always at the back of my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But during the time when you were at the police, when you say "Many," is it that 20, 50, 100.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't say. Each investigation I attended, during each such an investigation, I analysed the direction of firing. Sometimes I couldn't be precise, especially, for example, when it comes to mortar shells. Say a mortar shell ricochets off of something, and there was an example of that when a shell flew through a -- to the branch of a tree, and what you could see on the asphalt was -- were traces which would point to the fact that it was fired from the direction of a certain wall nearby, which made no sense. It fell less than a metre away from the wall of a building; therefore, if you were only to look at the traces, it would seem as if the shell had been fired from the direction of the building, which is one metre away, and that is impossible. As for the number of analyses, well, I'd say 50 or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for giving to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now, and as I indicated the technicians have work to do and require half an hour break. So we we'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state for the record your, name your full name.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: My name is Ismet Hadzic; father's name Dervis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I am a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is there a reason for that, given your young age?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the compliment, but there is no special reason. I went to earlier retirement due to the reorganisation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's his ages. What's your age?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What's your age, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1952; therefore, now I'm 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before the war, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I worked at the company called Energoinvest, and I was a specialist for checkup of engines without intrusive method into that their work. It is a type of mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did you live at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: In 1984, after the Olympics, I was given an apartment in the Novo Naselje, the New Olympic settlement in Dobrinja, and I lived in Dobrinja since that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So during the war, you continued to live in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now during the conflict, and I am talking about 1992 to 1995, did you have a function within the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, 1992, I was appointed commander of the 1st Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have any qualifications to become the commander of a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was a person of some authority, but I held no military qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1971, I was in Zagreb to serve my military term. I was enlisted with the Rocket Anti-aircraft Defence. I worked on the SAM 2 Russian-make systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. Now, as you know, the Trial Chamber is mainly concerned with the time frame of the second part of 1994 and 1995. But can you briefly answer a few questions about the way the war developed, starting in 1992, in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja, in terms of geographic location, is placed between the Sarajevo airport and the Mojmilo hill. In late 1991, there were hundreds of tanks going to the Lukavica barracks through Dobrinja. There were also APCs and lots of material and equipment while the JNA was withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia. The citizens of Dobrinja, naive as they were, waived to the soldiers and threw flowers on the tanks. The situation was different at that time. The people who arrived at the barracks then would appear in the local cafes; and as early as the beginning of 1992, they started making problems and getting into fights with the people who regularly attended those cafes. The peak of it all, or rather, when we all came to our senses was when the APCs and tanks were brought to the Mojmilo hill in mid-March 1992. I believe there were three tanks, two APCs, as well as the equipment and soldiers, and they took up positions at Mojmilo hill near the water reservoir. And, thus, they held about 50 per cent of all water supply for the city of Sarajevo. When they took up position there, they put up the flag of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And let me briefly interrupt you there. Was there a time when Dobrinja was cut off from the rest of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja was cut off on the 4th of March, when a checkpoint was established. It was surrounded completely. They used tree trunks and other things, thus, physically preventing any movement between Dobrinja and the rest; and then Dobrinja and Mojmilo hill and the airport, which had already been taken by the Serb forces, and then with Kula and Lukavica on the other side, we were completely encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And later that early summer, was there a time when people started leaving from Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: On the 13th or 15th of May, over the loud speakers of the JNA or the RS or the Serb forces, one could hear an invitation, or rather, a message for the inhabitants of Dobrinja to move out. Two settlements had already been emptied; these being Dobrinja 4 and Drobrina 1B. So that message was sent in the morning, and at around 11.00, those who were ready to leave left. In our assessment, on that day, with the assistant of the Serb forces, some 4.000 Dobrinja inhabitants left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how long people were living in Dobrinja before the war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: As I said, at first, Dobrinja comprised three segments; the right, the centre, and the left section. It had 12 and a half thousand apartments and around 45.000 inhabitants. A good example would be that the mean age at Dobrinja was between 28 and 30. The population was quite young.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And maybe my last question about that period, after the people left, these 3, 4.000 people, was there shelling that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Not on that day. Early the following day, heavy shelling started, indiscriminatory shelling as if it were raining. After that, an infantry attack followed from the area of Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. I think that's enough for the background. Let's turn to the Dobrinja Brigade. You told us earlier that on the 6th of July 1992, you were appointed the commander of the 1st Dobrinja Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now when was the brigade formed, on the same day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of July, a courier arrived over Mojmilo hill carrying a sealed envelope, saying that the presidency of the Bosnia and Herzegovina had appointed me commander of this brigade. By that time, all other brigades were formed except from our brigade. So we were the last to have received an order to form a brigade. Upon receipt of this order, I tried to find men who were versed in military matters and who were capable of establishing a mountain brigade as the order stipulated. I was lucky to find Colonel Beslagic, who was in the air force, and it took him about two or three days to set up a brigade from his memory only. It wasn't a proper brigade, but some 89 per cent was there of our requirements. Based on his experience, we tried to find men who had been in the JNA, in order to expand the brigade and to have all the structures required as per establishment. And to tell you the truth, it was very difficult because we had to find 2.000 men at once, and we didn't have any lists of people living in the neighbourhood. You had to provide food and clothing for men, and there was no weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So when you say that you found 89 per cent, you mean 89 per cent of 2.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honours, on the paper and as per establishment, it did not correspond to the actual establishment, so it was 80 percent accuracy as to what a brigade is stipulated to have on paper per establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is a brigade required to have as per establishment, so I can know how many men you actually had? That's what I want to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had battalions, it had a staff, staff units, staff attached units, everything that goes together with battalions; medical units, quarter master service, logistics, everything that constitutes a military formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But in terms of numbers, how many men did you actually have in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Upon finalising the whole process, we had about 2200 men, after we finished the mobilisation or call-up process. We had 2200 men, because that is a mountain brigade as per establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many were you supposed to have in a proper brigade.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Approximately, that same number. According to establishment, proper establishment prescribed on the paper, a company should perhaps have three medical detachment, and we had one detachment for one company. And that satisfied the needs of one company. One medical detachment satisfied the needs of one company. The same applied to people who were in charge of logistic supply, food supply, et cetera, because the -- the whole process was made easier because the zone was not such an expanded one. If you allow me to finish this, the whole process from the time we received the order until we somehow wrapped it up lasted for less than two months. The solemn oath was taken towards the end of August, and at that time we had a properly established brigade, area of responsibility was assigned to it, and we were able to deploy men in this area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Witness, what did you have in terms of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had very few weapons. We had homemade rifles, hunting rifles, trophy weapons. Lucky were the ones who were able to purchase an automatic rifle or a pistol. And we also had some other homemade devices or makeshift devices with explosives and things like that, in order for to us to cope with the situation that we found ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We will go back to weaponry a little bit later and also talk about mortars. But for the time being, let's just focus on the early period in 1992. Did you read any books in -- in preparation of establishing this brigade.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: When I received an order on the assignment, I started looking for military literature in order to educate myself better for the position, and I did manage to find some with people who were in this field. I was most helped with the British lexicon on military issues. It had ten volumes, and I managed to find everything that we needed there. The fact is that we couldn't apply the tactics and other instructions from these books on the ground. I said that many time that through a kind of illogical warfare, we confronted trained army people and we somehow, through this illogical warfare, managed to come out victorious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just to make it clear, can you tell the Trial Chamber why was it necessary to establish a brigade in Dobrinja in mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I already said that we were encircled already in May, that there were many volunteers loitering around, there were so many informal groups, and it was very difficult to coordinate all these issues. We were encircled. The Serbian forces attacking, entering Dobrinja, taking people away, et cetera. Simply speaking, there was no hierarchy or command or control. There were attempts to establish a battalion from among the ranks of the Territorial Defence, but I think that they created even more chaos than before. And they created the necessity of linking up all of these scattered elements, and that would be a guarantee for us to survive in Dobrinja. And I think that the forming of the Dobrinja brigade was a water shed in this totally chaotic situation that prevailed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you told us that the brigade was called the 1st Dobrinja Brigade. Did it change its name throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The brigade was initially called the 1st Dobrinja Brigade. I think towards the end of 1992, following reorganisation in the army, we received an order to form a 5th Motorised Brigade. In late 1993, another battalion was attached to us that had been part of the 101st Brigade, and the area of responsibility was thereby expanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the name of your brigade in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: There was another reorganisation in 1994, and the brigade was renamed 155th Mountain Brigade. And if I may add one more thing, until the end of the war, there was another change in name. And until the Dayton Accords were signed, the brigade was called the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did that last change occur, from 155th Mountain Brigade to the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: In late 1995 or beginning 1996, that was the time when the command was moved from Dobrinja, because in actual fact two brigades merged; 101st and 155th. And the 125th emerged from these two brigades. And it was in the Viktor Bubanj barracks or the Ramiz Salic barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask whether the word "motorised" in the new name had any significant, whether in terms of how the brigade was organised or in terms of the kind of weapons that it had at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, this reform only entailed the change of number of troops; however, the weapons remained the same. Motorised [as interpreted] brigades had around 2.000 men, and Motorised brigade had between 3800 and 4.000 men and they had weapons of standard issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just following up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that there was chaos, there were several brigades, several groups of soldiers that needed coordinating. Does this mean that your brigade played the role of military police or police in the settlement, or was it to fight against the Serbs, and did it indeed fight against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't have a role of a military police, but rather to defend the local residents. These groups or individuals in various parts of Dobrinja were supposed to be put under one cap, under one command in order for everyone to be able to survive in this neighbourhood. Many people from these groups were admitted into the regular formation of the 1st Dobrinja Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Defend the population against whom? Against the groups of citizens fighting against other citizens or against the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were defending ourselves from the army of Republika Srpska, which was an organised force, and we were encircled in the a most traditional way by a well organised army of Republika Srpska, or rather, Serbian forces, as they were called at the time, because Republika Srpska didn't exist at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I also see that once the appendix "mountain" appeared in the name of your brigade. Given that it was a fairly flat area in Dobrinja, why was it called the mountain brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: The Dobrinja Brigade, there were no mountains as far as I know. It's a flat area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Didn't you say that once the name of the brigade was the -- I think it was the 125th Mountain Brigade or something. You never used the word "mountain"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The 1st Dobrinja Brigade was a mountain brigade. That's how it was called according to establishment, according to the rules of service of the JNA. It wasn't related to any specific geographical area. That was the terminology that used to be used at the time. A mountain brigade was supposed to have a certain number of troops and equipment, or alternatively, motorised brigades were also defined in certain terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. Now let's move to August 1994. Now we have the 155th Motorised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many soldiers would say you have now in August 1994?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Around 4.000 men. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. No, no. We didn't have as many. Around 3.000 or -- between 3.000 and 3800.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So over time, since it started in mid-1992, you almost doubled the number of soldiers that were part of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yeah, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in 1994, mid-1994, how many battalions did you have in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: We had four battalions under arms; not all of them actually, but there were four battalions that were guarding the line at the foothill of Mojmilo, and there was always one battalion in the area of responsibility at Igman. Because after the conflict in 1993, we were assigned one part of the area of responsibility on Mount Igman. In addition to these four battalions, we had a logistical battalion, an engineers battalion, and everything to be expected according to the establishment for this kind of brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll come to location of these battalions in just a moment. My last question about the general setup is what was the ethnic composition of your brigade in the second half of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if at the same time, the exhibit ter number 03013 could be prepared, and I'm only interested in the last page of that range.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of your brigade in middle of 1994, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: We were a multi-ethnic brigade. We had 21 per cent of the others. The rest were Muslims or Bosniaks; 13 to 15 per cent were Serbs; the next largest group were Croats; there were also Hungarians and Romanies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, incidentally, what was the ethnic population of the population, the civilians in Dobrinja during the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact percentages, but it corresponded the composition of the brigade. The majority were Muslims. There were fewer Serbs in Dobrinja than Croats because some of the Croatian political parties tried to resettle the Croats from Dobrinja. We prevented that move, and asked the Croats to stay with us and they did. So there were Bosniaks, Croatians, Serbs, Hungarians, and Romanies, but I can't give you the percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hadzic. Now you see on the screen a map. Do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be scrolled to the bottom a little bit so that a signature appears.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this map. That's the map of Dobrinja, and the separation lines that we had facing the army of Republika Srpska from the beginning till the end of war changed almost not at all. So basically this is the area, and these are the separation lines between us and the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have the original of this -- this map which has been signed by the witness vis-a-vis investigator, which I would like to put on to the ELMO because you can see that it's coloured. So it might be a little bit easier for Your Honours to see that and for the witness to use the screen to emphasise these -- these lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On the screen now, Witness, do you see the original of the map that you had signed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And these red markings --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps if you could it could be turned a little bit so we can see the numbers, which appear in the middle the way they are supposed to be. Yes, but you need to open it. I think that's fine. The numbers are still upside down, but at least it's facing in the right way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, who marked these red lines here?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, first of all, can you explain, and using the screen in front of you, to the Judges the various parts of Dobrinja, and you mentioned a few already. You mentioned Mojmilo, you mentioned Mojmilo hill, and I think the airport as well. Can you use the screen, and now I'd like to go back to the electronic scanned version. Can you mark Mojmilo hill first.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: It's this area here, between the water reservoir to the right. That's the Mojmilo area, and it stretches further on to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You need to make a circle with that electronic pen around it.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, and please attach the letter A next to it.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if we can scroll up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you indicate to Their Honours where the settlement of Mojmilo is located?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: You can't see it on this electronic map. It's somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have a technical question to the registrar. If the witness marks outside the actual map, will it still be captured or thus his markings need to be on the map itself.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, it will be captured, but it's preferable that it's done within the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please put the letter A into the middle of the circle depicting Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now can you indicate to Their Honours where the airport is.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And please use the letter B to explain the line you just drew.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And could you lead Their Honours through these various parts of Dobrinja. I think you used Dobrinja 4 and Dobrinja 1B. Can you show to Their Honours where these settlements are.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja 4-1, and Dobrinja 4-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just marked two circles to the far right attaching the numbers 4 to it. Now, before you continue, you started -- in fact, you completed a circle just to the right of the airport area, the first one to the right. Can you attach a letter to it explaining what it was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to put a letter or a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, number C will be great.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: This letter C signifies Dobrinja 1A, and the next one is Dobrinja 1B. Which letter shall I use to mark it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mark with 1B.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do the other parts of Dobrinja also have names?

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do. This one adjacent to Dobrinja 1A is C5. Do you want me to circle it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: So this is C5 quarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please mark C5.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the next settlement to the left of C5, slightly up and left.

utterances.speaker: ISMET HADZIC
utterances.text: This is the so-called airport settlement, or Aerodromsko Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you attach the letter D to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I would like you to conclude this exercise, but I have to be mindful of the fact that Judge Mindua has to appear for another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We will continue tomorrow. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's not finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But we need to tender it, I guess; otherwise, it will be lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's give it a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be marked for identification as P328. JUDGE ROBINSON: Thank you. We will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
